Online Government Services—Log-on and Identity Verification Services
12. CHRIS AUCHINVOLE (National)  to the Minister of Internal Affairs : What
announcements has she made regarding th e igovt scheme, and making it easier for
people to verify their identities to government agencies?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: Last week the Electronic
Identity Verification Bill had its first read ing in the House. The bill will give New
Zealanders the option of an easy and secure way to verify their identities to access a
range of Government services. I was heartene d by the extensive cr oss-party support for
the bill’s first reading.

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: How will this service work in combination with the igovt log-on
service?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: The service allows people the choice of using one log-on to
access secure online services across multiple Government agencies without having to
repeatedly provide physical documents time and again. Under igovt, the process will be
streamlined while ensuring appropriate safeguards remain in place.
Overseas Investment Rules—Judicial Decision on Sale of Crafar Farms

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I call on order of—

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. I think you have another matter to d eal with, unless you are just going to call
Mr Parker straight away.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I thank the honourable member for his intervention, because indeed
I should consider this before  I call the Address in Reply debate. What has been lodged
is a letter. Letters seeking under Standing Order 386 an urge nt debate on matters can be
lodged up till—I mean, ideally lodged before the House sits. But I am not in any way
turning this application down because that was not the case; my understanding is it may
not even have been possible to achieve that.
What I am faced with here—and it is not ve ry often that the Speaker has to make a
decision on one of these on the hoof—is a letter  from the Hon David Parker that seeks
under Standing Order 386 that I allow an urge nt debate on the decision of the High
408 Urgent Debates Declined 15 Feb 2012
Court in Wellington that “The Ministers’ consent to the overseas investment to be made
by Milk NZ in the Crafar farms is set aside.” I feel able to make a ruling on this pretty
much on the hoof, because for an urgent debate on an issue to be allowed, the issue
must be an issue for which a Minister ha s direct responsibility. A Minister does not
have direct responsibility for a decision of th e court. That is not a matter the Minister
has direct responsibility for, and I believe on those grounds that  it is not appropriate for
me to allow that urgent debate.
I make it very clear that I am not turning it down on the ba sis of the slightly unusual
arrival of the application. I accept that the application is perfectly in order, but Ministers
are not responsible for decisi ons of the court. Urgent de bates can be allowed, and the
business of the House set aside under Standi ng Order 386, only for matters that are the
responsibility of Ministers.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. The triggering factor th at makes it urgent is certain ly the decision of the High
Court, but it was a decision of the High C ourt to overturn a mini sterial decision. What
this does is undo a ministerial decision and l eave a void where that decision was. Now,
if I were you I might turn it down on the fact that there is an Address in Reply debate
going on, and there is possibly an ab ility to deal with it there, or on the fact  that it can
be the subject of a later debate , but I am pretty sure that if we go back through some of
the precedents, we will see it is not the timing around the original decision; it is when it
comes to light and becomes urgent. And that , I understand, happened at some stage this
morning but was then reported. The other—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: Can I make one other point?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will hear the member.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: That point is, as Mr Parker has just pointed out to me,
that unless another amendm ent is moved—and it would be an interesting confidence
amendment—he cannot speak on it because, of course, he spoke yesterday in the
Address in Reply debate, as have some others.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Speaking to the point of order,
Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will hear the honourable Leader of the House.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I think that if you were to accept that argument from
Mr Mallard there would be numerous occa sions where ministerial decisions are
revisited one way or another—perhaps, so metimes, many, many years after the event
first occurred. So I think you are quite right in saying that the provisions for an urgent
debate in this House are for occasions when a Minister makes a decision that has very
significant public interest, and where there has been no other occasion for the House to
discuss the matter.
Now, this matter has been the matter of questions in the House. It has been the matter
of various bits of speculation in speeches in the Address in Reply debate, and, of course,
as Mr Mallard points out, we are still in th e Address in Reply debate. So I think you are
quite correct in maintaining the long-held vi ew or precedent that is reflected in the
Standing Orders that says it has to be a recent decision by the Government—by a
Minister, effectively—on which there has b een no other opportunit y, or there is not
likely to be any other opportunity, for debate . Further, I would point  out that although
you are saying you do not have to have the ap plication in by that time, the Standing
Order does say 1 hour before the House commences, and this  decision technically was
available within that time space.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Point of order—
15 Feb 2012 Urgent Debates Declined 409

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Speaking to the point of order,
Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I do not really need to hear a lo t more, but I will hear firstly from
the Rt Hon Winston Peters.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Just as a suggestion, there is a precedent for such a
ruling, and that is the injunction against —you remember—the All Black tour to South
Africa, where the ruling was given by th e judge favouring the injunction, whereupon
that triggered an urgent deba te in Parliament. I am not tr ying to gainsay your decision,
but there is precedent where that is exactly what happened.

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: Just very briefly, I would argue that
rather than looking backwards, as the members over here have suggested, it is actually a
question of ministerial responsibility. What th e courts have said is that the Ministers
must redo the decision. That is the minist erial responsibility. That is the specific
language that is used in the Standing Orders. There is now ministerial responsibility to
reconsider the decision; that is what the courts have directed them to do.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: Speaking to the point of
order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Very briefly I will hear the Hon Trevor Mallard.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: Although I hesitate to di sagree with the Rt Hon
Winston Peters, I think he might have had his argument slightly upside down. My
memory is that the House declined the debate on the injunction when it was granted,
and the reason that it was declined was that  it was an injuncti on between a group of
individuals and the Rugby Football Union,  for which there was no ministerial
responsibility. But in this case,  I do not think we could ha ve anything that was more
involved with ministerial responsibility. I th ink if you look at the accompanying
documents and go through them, you will see there is line after line where the court has
pointed out that ministerial responsibility a ppears not to have been exercised properly.
That, I think, when you have a court finding that Ministers are not doing their jobs
according to the law—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! No, I think we have heard su fficient on this. I do not need to
hear further on this.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. It is my
application.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I accept the point the Hon David Parker made there. It is his
application. I will hear him.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: There are three parts to the test laid out in Standing Order
386. The first is that it is a particular case of recent occurrence, and this clearly is. The
second is that it involves the administrativ e or ministerial responsibility of the
Government, and with regard to the Speaker’s  initial comments, I think, with respect,
that it does, and that the difference with the case of the Rugby Football Union that was
referred to is that was not a case of mini sterial responsibility. In my submission, Mr
Speaker, the decision for you is whether this  requires the immediat e attention of the
House, because the first two legs of the test are made out.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I thank the members for their contributions, because this is an
important issue of order. I appreciate the contributions. As the Hon Trevor Mallard
pointed out, in fact, the application way back in, when was it, 1980—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: —1985, was it? It was 1985, indeed. That application was turned
down on the grounds that the Hon Trevor Mallard has mentioned. The reason why I
have declined this application is that the case was not made for an urgent debate. This is
not a recent Government decision or action. What  has triggered this is the decision of a
410 Urgent Debates Declined 15 Feb 2012
court; that is what the applic ation is based on. The applicati on is specifically to debate
the decision of the High Court, and no Minist er is responsible fo r the decision of the
High Court.
What I am not ruling is that the issue is not important, or that it is not possible to
frame an application that might meet the St anding Orders. But it is my view that this
application does not meet the requiremen t of the Standing Orders, because this
application is to set aside the business of the House to debate the decision of the High
Court, and that is not a respons ibility of a Minister. That is why I believe we have to be
very careful not to allow setting aside of the business of the House for actions that are
not the responsibility of a Minister—and this one is not. The application is based on the
decision of the court. But it does not rule out further applications.
What I am saying is the application in fr ont of me, in my view, does not meet the
test. But just because an application has been made today does not mean to say that it is
not possible to make further applications. Members may recollect, in fact, that there was
an issue in the last term where I finally did consider that an application met the test. It
might have been the third application on a pa rticular issue. So this does not rule out
future applications. It is just in my view t oday—I have to be careful . In this particular
application I am not in any way belittling the issue, it is just that the way this
application is made does not meet the test, because we cannot set aside the business of
the House to debate a decision of the High C ourt. On that basis I must decline this
application.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I seek the leave of the House
to set aside time for such a debate.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought for that course of action. Is there any objection?
There is objection.
Debate resumed from 14 February.

items.speaker: Dr JACKIE BLUE
items.text: It is a true pleasure to speak in this Address in
Reply debate. The Government was elected in the general election with a mandate to get
on with the business of making New Zealand a successful place to live, work, and bring
up our children. New Zealand is better placed than most countries. The debt crisis in
Europe, in countries like Greece, demonstr ates what happens wh en you do not act on
debt. The National-led Government believes th at as a country we must get our debt
under control and balance our books. This is crucial to allow us to grow our economy,
create local jobs, and enjoy higher wages. The National-led Government is determined
to keep on top of debt, keeping it below 30 percent of GDP. We have been and will
continue to be responsible managers by restri cting debt. We are determined to get back
into surplus, and we have a plan over th e next 3 years to build  solid foundations for
growth and more jobs.
We have made a great start. Across the board income tax has more than compensated
the vast majority of income earners for the rise in GST, meaning they have more money
in their pockets to spend. Around three-quarters  of earners now pay a top tax rate of no
more than 17.5 percent on their income. The average wage has increased 10 percent in
the past 3 years, and that is taking into account tax and inflation. Superannuation
payments have gone up 19 percent over the past 3 years, around double the rate of
inflation. The married couple rate for s uperannuation, for example, has gone up $166 a
fortnight in 3 years. We are working hard  to lift the long-term performance of the
economy, create jobs, and create an environment that encourages economic growth.
15 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 411
We are focused on protecting jobs while en suring a fair wage. I am particularly
pleased with the 90-day trial period in troduced by our Government. In 2008 we
introduced the 90-day trial period for em ployers with fewer than 20 employees.
Research by the New Zealand Institute of  Economic Research showed that 13,000 New
Zealanders got jobs thr ough the 90-day trial periods.  The Government has now
extended that 90-day trial period to all employe rs to enable New Zealanders to benefit
from it, and they will I am quite sure. It is good for people returning to the workforce or
those without a work history. It is good for youth, migrants, and women. Quite simply,
it is a win-win.
New Zealand is well placed to succeed and create more jobs for New Zealanders, but
we must back business. After all, it is bu sinesses that create jobs. The Minister for
Economic Development, Steven Joyce, recentl y wrote an excellent opinion piece in the
New Zealand Herald, and I would like to touch on this . He wrote that for New Zealand
to be successful we need more jobs and more higher-paying jobs. Jobs provide the
incomes that people use to help their familie s get ahead. Jobs give people the income to
pay taxes for the public services, like health  and education, that we value, and well-
paying jobs are what keep more of our people in New Zealand, contributing to our
country. And, of course, keeping families together means our communities are stronger.
But, critically, meaningful, sustainable jobs will depend on businesses that provide
services or products that people need or want. The Minister we nt on to say in the article
that businesses depend on six key things: ideas and innovation to create the business—
that is, entrepreneurs and ideas people—m oney to build the business; access to raw
materials; skilled people to work in the business; the public infrastructure that
businesses depend on, such as power, broa dband, and transport; and, most important,
customers who want to buy the product. Essentially, if we want more and better jobs for
New Zealanders, we need to encourage more businesses to be based here. To do that we
need to make sure those six key drivers are there and easier for bus inesses to access. It
is all about encouraging an environment that  is encouraging to en trepreneurs and ideas
people. We need to ensure that we make re sources available for businesses to use. We
need stronger and more internationally inte grated capital markets that provide money
for investment. We need to ensure that our pe ople have the right sk ills. And we need to
remember that we have a small domestic market, so our businesses will need to access
world markets a lot earlier than similar busine sses in countries located in larger world
populations.
The Minister wrote in the article that we need to start a “we can” culture and move
away from the “we can’t” culture. We need to reframe the argument to “why we
should” from “why we shouldn’ t”. It is about removing ro adblocks and obstacles. The
Minister went on to elaborate that this “can’t  do” attitude was the prevailing attitude in
the 2000s. Over that decade we progressively boxed ourselves in more and more, so we
depended on fewer and fewer industries base d on what the “can’t” group said. At the
end of the day, the Government of the day wa s pretty much down to talking about only
two of the key ingredients—that is, skill training and subsidising entrepreneurs who do
not use resources.
The Minister summed it up by saying that we “need to stop the endless debate about
which industry will save us and focus on all industries where New Zealand has a natural
advantage. That’s why the Government is implementing and further developing its 120-
point action plan that will he lp build a stronger, more co mpetitive economy.” We need
to encourage and develop all th e opportunities if we are to prosper. The article by the
Minister was extremely well written and thoughtful, and I encourage all my colleagues
to read it.
412 Address in Reply 15 Feb 2012
Another win-win for New Zealanders is th e mixed-ownership model, which we told
New Zealanders about a year ahead of the election. The G overnment owns about $220
billion of assets, and we are expecting to invest another $34 billion over the next 5
years. Rather than borrow more money to pay for this, we are extending the mixed-
ownership model to the four State-owne d energy companies—that is, Mighty River
Power, Meridian, Genesis, and Solid En ergy. We are reducing the Government’s
majority shareholding in Air New Zealand, which is already under a mixed-ownership
model, and has proven to be very successful . The public-private partnership model will
bring sharper commercial disc ipline and better-performing companies, as has happened
with Air New Zealand.
We have guaranteed to the New Zealand public that the Government will be the
majority shareholder and will maintain a minimum of a 51 percent shareholding stake.
There will be priority for Kiwi investors, which will allow individual shareholders to
hold around 10 percent, further ensuring Kiwi  control. It frees up between $5 billion
and $7 billion to invest directly into the Future Investment Fund for schools and
hospitals, and other productive assets. The mixed-ownership model will help balance
the books by 2014-15 without extra borrowing. A nd it does put Kiwis at the front of the
queue for shares and investments other than finance companies. We are confident that
these companies will remain overwhelmingly in New Zealand control. We expect New
Zealanders will own at least 85 to 90 percent of these companies. That is because the
Government will keep 51 percent majority control. It is a good investment opportunity.
New Zealand investors have about $100 billion sitting in term deposits, and there are
tens of billions of dollars i nvested by other New Zealand inve stors, such as KiwiSaver,
the New Zealand Superannuation Fund, ACC, the Government Superannuation Fund,
and iwi.
We will be able to fund new assets such as broadband, schools, and hospitals without
borrowing more. We told New Zealanders ab out our plan a year ahead. There was no
subterfuge. We were upfront and clearly spelt out our plan. It is a smart policy that will
strengthen New Zealand’s economy, and a st ronger economy is the only way we will
create jobs, boost incomes, and provide high -quality public services  that New Zealand
needs. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon TARIANA TURIA
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Assistant
Speaker Tisch. T ēnā tātou katoa. In the Speech from the Throne there was one simple
statement that revealed the next steps in  progressing our transformation agenda. As
agreed with the M āori Party, a separate appropriation and governance structure will be
established for Wh ānau Ora. This statement was a signal to us all that Government has
confidence in Wh ānau Ora as an approach that is premised on delivering better results
for w’ānau. In the relationship accord  that confidence is articu lated further: “to support
the evolving focus and ongoing implementation of Whānau Ora.”
Today I want to share some of our lear ning and our successes in the journey of
w’ānau transformation. The sheer numbers of w’ ānau engaged is one tangible measure
of the enthusiasm with which New Zeala nd families are taking up these opportunities.
We have 25 provider collectiv es representing 160 provide r organisations currently
delivering to, and engaging, w’ ānau and families. At least 2,000 w’ ānau plans,
representing more than 15,000 fam ily members, have set their w’ ānau planning
activities in motion thr ough involvement in the Wh ānau Integration, Innovation and
Engagement Fund. In addition, 1,000 w’ ānau are actively navigated to access existing
services through our 25 provider collectives.
But although the numbers are important, th e overriding interest for me has been the
outcomes. Are we seeing successful w’ ānau across a broad range of situations? Let us
15 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 413
be clear: this is high-risk business with a potential for a high return. There is no quick-
fix solution to achieve the well-being of families.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. In accordance with
numerous Speakers’ rulings and Standing Or ders, I ask that the member table the
speech instead of reading it.

items.speaker: Hon TARIANA TURIA
items.text: Let us be clear: this is hi gh-risk business with a potential
for high return. There is no quick-fix solution to achieve the well-being of families, but
we have to invest time, energy, and resources in family to be self-managing.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! We have a point of order
from the Hon Trevor Mallard. I ask the member to resume her seat, please. The decision
of the Standing Orders Committee late la st year, which is now to be commonplace
within the House, is that speeches are not to be read. That is why the Hon Trevor
Mallard asked that the speech be tabled. We  can refer to speeches but we cannot read
them verbatim. So I ask the member in her remaining time to use it as guidance for her
speech rather than reading it verbatim. She can  just refer to it in the context of which
she wishes to speak this afternoon.

items.speaker: Hon TARIANA TURIA
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. We were not advised
of the change to the Standing Orders to say that speeches could not be written and
spoken to in the House, and—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I ask the member to resume her
seat. Last year, the last thing before the House adjourned was th at the new Standing
Orders of Parliament were ac tually adopted by the House. So  from this year on, this is
what is going to be the accepted practice. If you are hearing this for the first time, I say
to all members that in future  they must only refer to thei r speech notes, as opposed to a
Minister who may be speaking directly to a bill in their name. The exception also was
for new members who are making their maiden  speeches. That is the ruling, and I ask
the member to just use the notes that she ha s as reference points for the balance of her
speech.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. One other point is that it
was a decision of the Standing Orders Committee, on which Mr Flavell was her
representative.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: I am wondering whether we can get around this, because it is
obviously a new Standing Order. It has obviou sly passed some of us by, and maybe,
with the good grace of the House, now that we do know we could start tomorrow afresh.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: In order to join my friend in his suggestion, rather than start
tomorrow, maybe it could be from the end of this speech. I seek leave for the Minister
currently reading her speech to be allowed to complete her speech reading it.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought for that purpose. Is
there any objection? There is no objection.

items.speaker: Hon TARIANA TURIA
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant Sp eaker, and thank you to the
House.
I would dare anyone in this Chamber to decl are raising families to be a walk in the
park, because we all know the challenges that come with raising children in today’s
world. The circumstances of daily life can at times be very stressful, even for the best of
families, and for some families their circumstances become overwhelming. There are so
many compounding factors, with poverty underpinning most factors. Successive
administrations have attempted to intervene in circumstances of crisis, but too many
times the intervention itself has simply created another obstacle in the path of the family
in need. A brave Government would admit that  the State is not the ultimate solution; a
bold Government would be prepared to put it s trust in the people, to acknowledge their
potential, and to enable w’ānau to set their own direction to make change happen.
414 Address in Reply 15 Feb 2012
This, indeed, is the hub of the political ch allenge: to find the point of equilibrium
between prudent accountability of public f unds, and an environment to support the
diversity of w’ ānau aspirations. I want to remind those who have spoken out in anger
against what they see as a one-man crusade to undermine Whānau Ora that Whānau Ora
has always been about more than politicians  and political parties. Indeed, it has never
relied on Parliament as a moral guarantor, a nd nor should it, for essentially the success
of Wh ānau Ora has been due to a rising tide of confidence in local solutions that we
trace back over many, many decades. It has emerged from the momentum of w’ ānau to
create a secure foundation fo r our mokopuna to benefit from, and the majority of our
w’ānau do this without State intervention.
Whānau Ora did not just come along in 2012. We  saw the genesis of the approach in
Pūao-te-ata-tū, in Tū Tangata, in the kōhanga reo movement, and in the Hui Taumata of
1984. The call was broad for w’ ānau, hapū, and iwi to determine, run, and control their
own initiatives. The funding for these moves would come from the so-called negative
spending that went into picking up the pieces.
A fundamental premise in this journey was to encourage the State to place faith in
the capacity of families to achieve outcomes th at could lead to their full participation
within society. This has not changed, a generation on, in our current environment,
where there has been significant change in our economic, social, and cultural
environment.
This journey is predicated on an investment  in an indigenous approach, an approach
based on M āori cultural foundations, built round a communal approach to well-being.
Indeed, it has been available to all who want to participate in this approach, and we have
been there before. Indeed, in this House 21 years ago, in April 1991, a politician rose in
the appropriation debate to give voice to a view that might well have come out of
Whānau Ora. The Minister of Maori Affairs at that time said that “It was not for central
government to determine for tribes their shap e, their character, or their form—and that
policy was supported by M āoridom. The Government woul d work in a voluntary way
with every tribe, with every subtribe, even  with family, but it would be oppressive and
culturally offensive to hol d out the taxpayers’ cheq ue-book and say, ‘Either you
conform or we don’t deal with you.’.” That politician was Winston Peters, and I hope he
can appreciate the contribution that Ka Awatea also made to a journey that we are now
seeing the fruits of through the success of Whānau Ora.
I said before that Whānau Ora is a high-risk business. Why would it not be, when we
know the impact that circumstances can have  on already fragile lives? But if it is high
risk it is also high return, and that return  has been evidenced in  three ways. We have
seen strategic leadership and regional championing, bringing t ogether knowledge,
expertise, and experience of community me mbers and Government processes to benefit
the well-being of w’ ānau. We are observing systemic change, progressive and
incremental success, demonstrated by integr ated contracts, multi-year funding, multi-
year planning, and the accompanying action re search to inform quality improvement
and to evidence outcomes. Most importantly , we are seeing the value, benefit, and
success of w’ ānau transformation as they build thei r capability and become the vehicle
for their own change.
Whānau Ora is about transforming our futures. It is being realised in outcomes across
social, cultural, and economic dimensions. On e of the most significant aspects is the
planning to create intergenera tional transfers of knowledge and values, to put an end to
cycles of despair, and to pave a way in which w’ānau aspirations are able to be fostered.
Our next steps are in extending Wh ānau Ora to the Kaipara, Hauraki, South Waikato,
Taupō, Tūrangi, Palmerston North, Wairarapa, Levin, the K āpiti Coast, and Murihiku.
We are championing an inclusive approach—a n approach that is driven by a focus on
15 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 415
outcomes—and that approach, although funda mental to the opport unities and gains for
w’ānau, also comes back to Government.
And so I conclude my contribution today with an assurance to the House that we can
have every confidence in the Wh ānau Ora approach, and that it will continue to evolve.
Despite the amount of resourci ng distributed acro ss Government departments and to a
range of agencies, there is an unfair expectation that Wh ānau Ora is the panacea for
everything. We all have the responsibility to be responsive, and to practise wh ānau ora.
It can begin with us all modelling hope, and placing value in a vision for tomorrow—
the translation of our hi ghest hopes into strong w’ ānau who will lead communities
throughout Aotearoa. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: I suppose that I am the first member of
the House to follow and operationalise this new ruling. I can assure  you, Mr Assistant
Speaker Tisch, and the House th at I will not be reading from a speech, but I will be
referring to a document that I think will become quite important in New Zealand’s
economic history over the next few years, which is the National Government’s 2011
national Economic Development Action Plan.
One of the things that I ha ve found very amusing coming from the other side of
politics—and I would say that perhaps the word “bemused” rather than “amused” is a
more appropriate word—is the accusation that National does not have a plan to fix New
Zealand. This is wrong on multiple levels, a lthough one is rather in terested that the
problem that we are trying to fix is the pr oblem we inherited from three terms of the
previous Labour Government. But I will put that  aside, try to deconstruct the criticism,
and ask what would constitute a plan.
I mean, is it some sort of hairy-ches ted 1950s version of it, with “Commissar
Cunliffe” or “Commissar Parker” working lo ng into the night with Leontief input-
output tables, allocating resources in the so -called public interest? I do not suppose that
is what they have in mind when they talk about an economic plan. So we would have to
assume that, on the basis that it is better to listen—

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speake r. I draw your attention to the fact
that members of this side of the House we re referred to as comm issars. I think that
although the member himself has acknowledged once being a Stalinist, it is out of order
in this House to call people on the opposite benches commissars.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I thank the member. I just ask the
member to withdraw that comment.

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: It will be the last time th at I will use—even obviously in
jest—the word “commissar”.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member has been asked
to withdraw the comment. That is all th e member is required to do, with no further
comment.

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: I withdraw and apologise.
So if that is not the concept of an economic plan, what would be the plan that Labour
has in mind? One would have to assume—on th e basis of the well-known principle that
people should be judged by the actions they take rather than on their words—that we
would look at the three terms that the New Zealand public did give to Labour the
confidence of the Treasury benches, in orde r to work out what a Labour-planned “fix
New Zealand” would look like.
So what would that really  add up to? Well, fundamenta lly, the plan that Labour
unleashed on New Zealand after 3 years in  the late 1990s—when growth averaged 4
percent, unemployment was rattling down, and the deficit was coming down at the same
time—resulted after 8 or 9 years in the follo wing basic economic facts. First of all, the
last 3 years of that Govern ment resulted in economic grow th under 1 percent, finally
416 Address in Reply 15 Feb 2012
achieving the remarkable distinction of pu tting New Zealand as the only developed
country in the world to be in recession be fore the Lehman Brothers collapse provoked
the global financial crisis.
It was an economic plan that gave us mo rtgage interest rate s of over 10 percent,
costing households on a typical average mo rtgage $200 a week more than they are
typically paying today on a struct ured mortgage of that nature . It was a plan that led us,
as we discovered in question time today, to an explosion of privat e sector debt from
around $70 billion in 1999 to  around $177 billion by Dece mber 2008, causing a huge
spike in New Zealand’s net international liabilities, which, as the Minister for Economic
Development pointed out today, has come down very remarkably, considering how
difficult it is to turn around a supertanker like that, from 85 percent of GDP to 69
percent of GDP. And it led to a tanking of productivity. So if that is the plan in Labour’s
mind, could it please find another country to experiment on than ours.
What we have given is a real plan, which is worki ng with New Zealanders and
working with the market to try to fix some of the immediate macroeconomic imbalances
facing New Zealand, and to make serious progress on long-term structural reform,
against the background of very  difficult domestic conditions caused by the Canterbury
earthquake, which is the second- largest insurance di saster in the history of the planet,
according to what I read—unbelievably—and, secondly, the global financial crisis. And
that is exactly what this Government has done  in the previous 3 years and will continue
with relentlessly over the next 3 years while  we have the confidence of the Treasury
benches. It will address those serious structural imbalances and, yes, it will indeed try to
lay the structural foundations for a brighter  long-term outlook for our economy and for
the people of New Zealand.
First of all, we have addressed many of  the structural economic imbalances, though I
will be the first to admit there is a long way to go. We have stopped what was intended
to be an endless spray of defici ts and have got a plan that wi ll have us just  crossing the
line into surplus by 2014-15. We have initiated on the structural side very long-overdue
tax reform, which involved a very much-needed shift on higher consumption—

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I am loath to interrupt the
member who has just returned to his seat, but I do seek the opportuni ty to table a copy
of the Government’s Economic Development Action Plan, noting that it contains no
mention—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Sit down. That is not a point of
order. You are interrupting the member speaki ng, and we are going to  hear the Minister
out. If you wish to seek leav e to table after the Minister  has spoken, you may. That was
a straight-out interruption of a member speaking.

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: In addition to moving on the macroeconomic front, the
economic plan that the member has just referred to advances a whole set of propositions
under more than 30 different h eadings of structural reforms, which piece by piece will
indeed create the foundations for improved economic performance in this country.
This is not the first time we have moved in this direction. If one  looks at our record
in the previous Government one could pick many examples. One, at random, would be
the work that we have done on aquaculture. After 8 or 9 years of not a single square
metre of fresh open water space being allocate d to what should be a far more vibrant
export industry for New Zealand, finally we have advanced the frontier of reform in this
area. It is just one small example of the structural reforms that this National-led
Government has advanced and intends to advance in the future. We have got the deficits
under control, though we have some way to go, and it will be a very difficult task to
continue to keep fiscal discipline at the point where we have got  restoration of New
Zealand into a prudent situation.
15 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 417
The one thing that is very clear is that the era of beer and skittles is over. It is time
now to get serious with public finances. Th ere is any number of signals around the
world telling New Zealanders, telling people of all nationalities, that that is the nature of
the game. This Government is serious. This is a vital component of our economic plan
for New Zealand. In addition to this, we have got a plan for advancing structural reform
under many of those headings in that documen t. They cover numerous different issues,
such as science and innovation, such as broadband and communications.
Rebuilding Canterbury is still a central preoccupation in terms of our economic plan
for New Zealand, as it must be, given that Ch ristchurch is the sec ond-largest city in
New Zealand and absolutely central to our expo rt effort. I want to give credit to the
people of Canterbury for maintaining an astonishing performance in terms of getting
their world-class goods and services out of  Lyttelton Port and out of Christchurch
International Airport, under the most stressful conditions. I think they have done just an
absolutely outstanding job and I think it is extraordinary, when I listen to the people
responsible for Lyttelton telling us that actually they are almost at record levels.
But we have a whole series of economic plans that we will be implementing,
including trying to move our time limits on consenting medium-term projects, and
freshwater reform. We are going to try to  address better the pl anning process around
assessing natural hazards. I predict that the Labour Party will oppose probably every
single one of those reforms. This, by the wa y—let me make it clear—is a prediction I
would love to be proven wrong on. But I am not counting on it; I am not counting on it.
Fundamentally, to conclude, this is about advancing the frontier of a wealth creation
economic plan for this country and trying to cap ture what I think is not just a necessity
but a mood shift that is there inside our  community and inside communities around the
world, as this process of financial dele veraging should be reaching every single
responsible political pa rty in this country. Finally, to put it in the metaphor that our
Prime Minister put it, we have indeed proven over the first 10 years of the 21 st century
that we can spend like a First World countr y. Now is the time to prove we can earn like
one. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: The member who has just resumed his
seat, Mr Groser, claimed to have a plan. Well, he and I attended, in  November, a
meeting of Business New Zealand where two- thirds of those present, New Zealand
businessmen, condemned the Government fo r having no plan. Although I waited with
much anticipation for the Speech from the Throne following the election, I have to
concur with the media verdict that this Speech from the Throne told us very little. It told
us nothing about where the Government want ed to go. There was no vision, no sense of
direction, and no plan—and that is rather sad.
I want to correct the member on one ot her thing. He claimed that National had
inherited a poor legacy. That is not what Bill English said on becoming Minister of
Finance. He said we were in good shape because a Labour Government had prepared
for the rainy day, which was the global financia l crisis. The fact is we had paid off our
debt. We had zero net Government debt. Now National is borrowing to the tune of $300
million a week. We had the lowest rate of unemployment in the OECD, and we had a
credit rating that the agencies put up, not down, which was their verdict on the adequacy
of the National Government’s response.
Mr Assistant Speaker Tisch, can I acknowledge your election to your position as
Assistant Speaker and also welcome new members to the House. I congratulate them on
their election. Can I particular ly congratulate the four ma iden speakers for Labour, who
gave, I believe, great speeches last night. Th ey talked of their vision, of where they had
come from, and about why they were in this  House and where they wanted our country
to go in order to be a fairer  and more effective country for all New Zealanders—and I
emphasise “all”.
But today I want to focus on a moment ous decision made in the High Court by
Justice Miller. What Justice Miller did, just  2 hours ago, was set aside a decision made
by Ministers Coleman and Williamson to sell 8,000 hectares of some of New Zealand’s
best dairy land to foreign investors. He set it aside, and thank God that we have got a
High Court judge with the gut s, under law, to stand up and act in New Zealand’s
interests when weak and incompetent Nationa l Party Ministers had failed to do so. The
judge was absolutely clear in his conclusion that the Ministers’ decision was thoroughly
inadequate. He said that the Overseas Invest ment Act requires the benefits of foreign
investment to be identifiable and substant ial, but that the Ministers had failed—had
failed—to ensure that the Sha nghai Pengxin Group application me t that test. In fact, he
was scathing about the Ministers’ decisions. He said that the Ministers had “misdirected
themselves”. That was his learned legal opinion. He said they had ignored the clear
evidence that benefit would accrue if the land remained in New Zealand’s ownership.
There was no need to sell it, he said. Th e Ministers ignored th e benefit that would
accrue if it remained in New Zealand’s owne rship, and he said that they had accepted
evidence about the economic benefit of the Shangha i Pengxin Group sale that was
materially overstated. In othe r words, the judge was very cl ear that the Mi nisters failed
to do their job. They let New Zealand down, and in that they were aided and abetted by
Prime Minister John Key.

items.speaker: Mr Key argued this
items.text: “The law would not have allowed us to reverse the decision
made by the Overseas Investment Office.” Not only was he wrong but he was proven
wrong in law. Far from the law not allowing the Overseas Investment Office to not
accept the application, he said th e law required it to look at criteria that should have led
it to reject that application. Mr Key wa s absolutely wrong, but  he will not accept
responsibility. I have been in  this House for a fair l ong time. The last person who
15 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 419
exhibited the characteristics of Mr Key was one Sir Robe rt Muldoon. He was wrong,
was proven wrong, but he was never prepared to accept responsibility for wrong
decisions and misstatements of fact that he had made.
In fact, the obligation on the Ministers wa s to ensure that they exercised their
judgment over this purchase bid, not to be  the puppets of the Overseas Investment
Office, which Mr Key implied when he said that they were simply following the
Overseas Investment Office’s advice. They do not get paid a quarter of a million dollars
a year to rubber-stamp what the Overseas I nvestment Office says; they are paid money
and given the responsibility to make decision s that are correct according to law and to
apply their judgment, and they failed absolutely to do that.
Then Mr Key claimed that the China free-trade agreement required that this decision
be approved. The judge’s decisi on explicitly rejects that and says that the Ministers
were advised that that was not correct. Th e Overseas Investment Act is an agreed
exception to the agreement in the free-tra de agreement that foreign and domestic
investors will be treated alike. It is speci fically set aside, and Mr Key is wrong and
misleads New Zealanders in claiming that the free-trade agreement required us to sell
out our heritage and pass ownership of that  land to this Shanghai-based company. Has
Mr Key—

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: How many pieces of farmland did you sell when you were the
Minister of Foreign Affairs?

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: —or Mr Henare—ignored the fact that no New Zealand
company can go to China and buy land in China? No New Zealand company can buy
land in China. I congratulate the Chinese on that, because the Chinese Government at
least can recognise that it needs to act in the interests of its own people—something that
the National Government in this affair has failed to recognise altogether.
Labour says that now is the time to draw a line in the sand. At the end of last year we
sold $100 million of prime land in Southl and, around where Mr English lives, to
German investors. Then the Government was intending to approve $200 million in the
sale of land to Chinese investors. I do not  care whether they are Chinese, German,
American, or whatever—

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: Oh yes, you do.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: —what I care about is whether th at decision was going to be in
the interests of New Zealand, and that is  where the High Court judge—I say to Mr
Henare—said absolutely that it was not in our interests. How can it be in our interests to
become tenants in our own land? John Key stood up and said that we will not become
tenants in our own land. What does he th ink happens when we sell off those 8,000
hectares of land, and the Shanghai Pengxin Group becomes the landlord and Landcorp
becomes the tenant? Is that not becoming tenants in our own land?
The fact is that that sale would not have increased our productivity and wealth, and it
would not have improved the way in which th e animals or pasture are managed; all it
would have done is push up the price for Kiwi farmers. It would have risked the value
added being transferred overseas, it would have risked transfer pricing where taxes were
paid not to our Government for activity in our country bu t to overseas Governments,
and it would have guaranteed that the money profits from our land flowed out of our
country to the benefit of foreign investors.
I want to say one other thing. It is about the sale of the State assets. Mr Key said that
the reason to do this was that he had a mandate to sell and that this would improve the
performance of the companies. Again, neither  is true. Massey Univ ersity did a properly
organised scientific survey. It  found that 75 percent of Kiwi s were against the sale of
our energy companies.

items.speaker: Hon Parekura Horomia
items.text: How many? How many?
420 Address in Reply 15 Feb 2012

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: Seventy-five percent were agains t it, and 9 percent were for it.
DigiPoll on Television New Z ealand last night found that 88 percent of the people
surveyed were opposed, and 8 percent were for it. There is no mandate, and if this
Government had the courage of  its convictions, it would take  this decision to a public
referendum to see whether or not it had its mandate. But it will not do that, because it
knows that at least three out of every four New Zealanders do not want to sell.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. T ēnā koe. Me tuku whakap āha ki a H ōnore Anne Tolley m ō taku
whakararuraru i tana k ōrero. Mr Speaker, e hiahia ana ki te k ōrero mō tētahi k ōrero i
kōrerohia e koe in ā tata nei i a au e ngaro an a. Ko te tikanga o taku t ū ake, ko te
āhuatanga o te k ōrero o te H ōnore Trevor Mallard ko tana i k ī mai, k āore i te tika kia
pānui mai t ētahi kōrero ki roto i te Whare, ki konei k ōrero ai i taua take. N ā, me p ēnei
rawa te k ōrero, kai te whakaae au ki te hiahia ki te k ōrero i runga i te ng ākau ā tēnā, ā
tēnā ēngari, i roto i te Standi ng Orders, kei reira tonu ētahi tikanga hai whai m ā tātou.
Ka huri ki te reo Pākehā i tēnei wā.
[Thank you. I need to apologise to the Minister the Hon Anne Tolley for the problems
I caused her during her address. Mr Speaker , I want to follow up a recent ruling you
made in my absence. The reason for rising and making this point of order relates to the
circumstances around what the Hon Trevor Mallard said when he stated that a member
cannot read his or her address in the Hous e but should deliver it in an impromptu
manner. I agree with that. Each member should speak from the heart, but there are
procedures in the Standing Orders for us to follow. At this point I switch to English.]
I just wanted to take up a matter raised earlier by the Hon Trevor Mallard and other
speakers coming in the debate, and I apprecia te that I have come  down from my office
to address this. It is to do with the issu e about the reading of speeches. Immediately
after that issue was raised, our office made an investigation and found that there is
actually, from our understanding, no mention of anything about not reading speeches, in
the Standing Orders. That is the first point. The second point is to raise, however, that in
the Speakers’ rulings—and I refer specifically to Speaker’s ruling 47/1, from September
2011—there is a phrase that states: “Where possible, members should not read speeches
… However, no member, other than the Sp eaker, may interrupt a member who is
speaking to suggest a breach of this conven tion, and the Speaker may allow speeches to
be read in some circumstances. Such circumstances may relate to the technical nature of
the material under discussion, or the relativ e experience of the member concerned.”
That was part of the Review of Standing Orders: Re port of the Standing Orders
Committee, September 2011, on page 28.
So there are two points I wanted to raise, wi th respect. The first one is, to correct Mr
Mallard’s discussion in Parliament, that  there is in fact no ruling, from our
understanding, from the Standing Orders Co mmittee about that convention. Secondly,
the onus is actually on the Speaker to make a decision, as opposed to a member of this
House. I raise that because Mr Henare and ot hers have spoken about  the fact that that
may set a precedent for the rest of our time ove r the next 3 years. I leave that for your
consideration.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I thank the member for his
comments. If we go back and look at the review of the Standing Orders, which was
tabled in the House and adopted by the Hous e, the point that the member makes, on
page 28, is correct, but the c onvention has been that we do  not read spe eches. If you
look at the opening statement there: “We also  wish to reiterate that, where possible,
members should not read speeches. The read ing of speeches was precluded until 1996,
and we wish to reassert this rule as a convention,”. So this was what was adopted by this
House on the review, and the member was a member of the Standing Orders review—as
15 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 421
I was—and understood the reasons  behind that. So what the tabling of this document,
the report of the Standing Orders Committee, and the accepting of it in the House is
actually doing is reasserting the convention that speeches should not be read.
Many members bring up points of  order. It is at the Speaker’s discretion whether a
speech should be read. I said to the memb er who was speaking, the Hon Tariana Turia,
that she should refer to her notes, so it wa s not as if I was sayi ng—I think I used the
word “verbatim”; it came up a couple of times . But then the House sought leave for her
to read it, and we were in the hands of th e House at that stage, and the House decided
that the Minister could read her speech. Th e points that the member has made are taken
on board, but I want to make it very clear th at the reading of speech es as pertained in
the report of the review of the Standing Orders—the convention that we do not read
speeches—is something that Speakers in the future, and the Chairman of the
Committee, will be looking at very closely. I thank the member for bringing that matter
to our attention.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. Sorry, Mr Assistant Speaker Tisch, not  to trivialise your response, but can I
just check with you, though, th e issue about—not being a lawyer—the difference
between a convention and a rule as set out by the St anding Orders. I as k that seriously,
because I understand the desire of the House at  that time and in the discussions to have
open, free debate, and I have got no problem with that. But the inference that Mr
Mallard gave—I thought; that I took from th e discussion—was that it was required, a
set rule, a Standing Order, and I am trying to make the point that that was not the case.
But if you could define “convention”, that would be helpful.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Well, I cannot; I am not a lawyer,
either. We need to get some advice on that. Can you just wait while I just ask the Clerk
for some advice on that matter.
The practice was part of the Standing Orders review. In the report it says that it is a
convention that speeches should not be rea d. This was adopted by the House, and I
mentioned that earlier on. There is no specific  Standing Order, I think that is a point for
the member—there is no Standing Order. But when the House adopted the report of the
Standing Orders Committee, which talks about  speeches being read, what it does is re-
enforces the convention or the practice that speeches  will not be read in the future. So
that is the position that this House adopted in  this report and that is what is going to be
the convention, which is going to be the protocol, as it were, from here on in. It does, of
course, allow for some flexib ility. I mentioned, when we discussed this earlier on, on a
point of order, that there will be Ministers who maybe can read a speech on a bill in
their name. It could be, and I mentioned th is also specifically, that new members
making their maiden statements will be able to read their speeches. There could well be
some technical aspects within a bill that re quire some explanation and that it would be
desirable that the person or the Minister actu ally read. I hope that clarifies the position.
It is a convention. We want to move back to an accepted practice that speeches in future
will not be read.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Is this on this point?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: It is on this point. It is pursua nt to this and I am not arguing
with your ruling. A second point of that new Standing Order then goes on to say that no
member other than the Speaker may interrupt  a member who is speaking, to suggest a
breach of this convention, and that is somethi ng that clearly has been broken. It is your
discretion and I would just hate to see th at there is a precedent set in this House
whereby we start down this track, as we have taken action on it.
422 Address in Reply 15 Feb 2012

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I thank the member. Yes, and I
acknowledged that earlier on th at it is at the Speaker’s discretion. I had made the
decision earlier on, and how it was resolved, finally, was that leave was sought. We are
in the hands of the House when leave is s ought for a particular co urse of action and I
think that was a resolution, a favourable resolution, for the Minister. I hope that ends the
matter.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: This National-led Government, of
course, has four key priorities for our s econd term as outlined by our Prime Minister:
first, to responsibly manage the Government’s finances; second, to build a competitive
and productive economy and lift, of course , the standard of living of all New
Zealanders; third, the rebuild of Christchur ch; and fourth, to deliver better public
services—and it is that last point that I,  as Minister of Po lice and Minister of
Corrections, want to talk a bout today and to expand on the Prime Minister’s address to
this House. Under National over the last 3 years, crime rates have fallen. My
predecessor, the Hon Judith Collins, oversaw immense improvements in corrections and
I want to confirm in the House today th at we remain firmly—firmly—focused on
preventing crime, reducing reoffending, and,  most important of all, keeping our
communities safe.
We are all aware that we are in very difficult economic times, so this is not just about
throwing money at problems; we do not have the money to throw at problems. It is
about working smarter, and one of the most  important and exciting initiatives to be
introduced by this National-led Government is Policing Excellence. This involves about
eight different streams of work that will see the police, and ha ve seen the police,
focusing more on crime prevention, making our  communities safer, reducing offending,
and all of that, of course, leads to fewer victims. That means fewer families grieving for
lost loved ones or being affected by white collar crime, which can, of course, have long-
term implications for people, as well as thi ngs as minor as burgla ries, which are a very
difficult emotional invasion for people no matter how small the issues are.
So Policing Excellence will increase the productivity and efficiency of our police,
and they have set themselves targets of a 13 percent reduction in reported crime. They
want to see more crime prevented before it ha ppens, so are looking for a decrease in the
amount of crime that happens, and, as a result  of that, a 13 per cent decrease in the
amount of crime that is recorded, and a 19 percent decrease in non-traffic apprehensions
resolved by prosecutions over the next 3 to 5 years. They are big targets for the police,
but they are determined to achieve those.
Amongst their work streams is Prevention First. This is where we are going to give
our police staff many more opportunities to be out there in communities, working in
areas where they know there are high risks, and looking to prevent crime before it
happens. When I talk to some of those front- line policemen out there, they say this is
the stuff that they joined the police to do. Th ey do not want to be arresting people; they
want to be making sure that they ar e stopping crime from happening. Neighbourhood
policing teams—32 of which have now been  deployed across the country—are again
working in areas where the intelligence tell s them the most crime is committed, where
young people are most likely to be congregatin g and getting into trouble. They are out
there working with those communities, coming up with all sorts of ways of preventing
crimes and making those communities safer.
Working on alternative resolutions, as an alternative to taki ng someone through the
court process, is rea lly important with our young people,  because the evidence is quite
clear that once we get those young people into that cycle of turning up at court, it is very
hard to get them out of it.
15 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 423
We are also looking at keeping our front- line police far more mobile. One of the
worst parts of their job is having to go back to the office and write everything up. So we
are looking at trialling technol ogy so that they can actually be  recording their actions at
the time. They do not have to stop what th ey are doing and go back into an office and
fill in forms. We are keeping them out there on the streets. So we are looking to increase
the number of hours that police are out there working on our streets.
And one of the last work streams is th e crime reporting line.  This is under way
currently in Auckland City, C ounties Manukau, and Bay of Pl enty and it is due to be
expanded this year. I have to say I had reason  to use this myself. The police are just a
phone call away. You do not have to go down to  the station and fill in forms; you can
talk to someone over the telephone, report the crime, give all the details, and get your
police number. It saves an awful lot of effort on behalf of the victims, particularly in my
area where rustling is a huge issue that has gr own over the last couple of years. Farmers
say to me: “Gosh, to report the crime, we’ve got to stop what we are doing, and we are
working, drive down the coast—it could be an  hour and a half or so to report the
crime—fill in the forms, and drive back.” Actually, they do not want to do that and soon
they will be able to pick up a telephone and report the crime.
So, in summary, Policing Excellence is putting more effort into crime prevention and
more hours into front-line policing, and that is leading to lower rates of offending and
that, of course, means that fewer people in our communities are the victims of crime—
and that is what we want. That is what we are focused on: reducing offending.
And, of course, we are interested in  reducing reoffending, because prisoner
rehabilitation is extremely important. When you look at the figures  for our prisoners,
you see that within a 12-month period, 45 percen t of prisoners released from prison are
reconvicted and 27 percent of them are re-imprisoned within 12 months of release. After
24 months—after 2 years—62 percent of them  are reconvicted, and 39 percent are re-
imprisoned. So there is a cycle that these peop le get on, and we are determined to make
sure that we can get more and more of them out of that cycle, back into their families
and their communities, and contributing to so ciety. So what have we done? Well, over
the last 3 years we have doubled the drug and alcohol treatment places for prisoners—
we have doubled them—and we will continue  to roll out more treatment places for
prisoners. We have boosted literacy a nd numeracy education in prisoners, which
languished under the previous Labour Government, and we have increased dramatically
the number of prisoners who are receiving work  skills training. It is so important that
they have those skills so that when they leav e prison, they are able to take their place in
the work force, and, of course, we are determin ed to work with them to make sure that
that happens.
Just last week, while I was visiting the Auckland Region Women’s Corrections
Facility, I spoke to offenders who were i nvolved in the distribution of food to other
prisons around New Zealand. They  not only have huge pride in  the work that they are
doing but are using that opportunity to gain their National Certifi cate of Educational
Achievement (NCEA) qualifications. The wo men I spoke to were aiming for their
NCEA level 2. They were pushing me to en sure that they could sit NCEA level 3—
there were some minor technicalities around the use of computers that we need to
resolve in order for them to achieve that. In fact, this week one prisoner in Christchurch,
I understand, has achieved the National Certificate in Distribution (Level 3). That means
that these women, when they leave prison, will have a skill that they can take with them
into the workplace. That gives them the oppor tunity then, using our 90-day trial period
legislation, to get that first j ob, to get that next step on the ladder th at gets them back
into the community and out of this cycle of reoffending and re-imprisonment.
424 Address in Reply 15 Feb 2012
We believe we have made enormous strides in corrections over the last 3 years, and
for that the management deserves credit. Th ey have done an outst anding job improving
the performance of our prisons and focusi ng on those reoffending rates—all part of
making our communities safer. Finally, can I refer to a report that was released a couple
of days ago showing that New Zealanders’ confidence in the New Zealand police force
has soared and that is simply a reflection of all the good work that this National-led
Government has done to support both th e police and corrections to make our
communities safer.

items.speaker: Hon LIANNE DALZIEL
items.text: May I begin by
acknowledging the re-election of the Speaker to his role. I have new portfolio
responsibilities: Canterbury earthquake recovery, civil defence and emergency
management, and consumer rights and standards.  I just want to say how grateful I am
for David Shearer’s confidence, because, w ith his background in disaster recovery, it
speaks a lot to me about what he has to offe r the city of Christchurch, and, indeed, the
country in terms of taking the lessons lear nt from Christchurch and making them our
own as a country.
We all know about disaster recovery. It re quires four particul ar things: quality
communication, community engagement, build ing resilience, but, most of all,
leadership. When I talk about leadership, th ere is a difference be tween the leadership
that is required in a response effort, whic h, of course, is command and control—people
need to do what they are told, they need to know that they can rely on the decision
maker—but in recovery it is di fferent. It is inclusive, it is engaging, it is a really
important way of ensuring that the community is able to go with those decision makers.
The Minister for Canterbury Earthquake Reco very has mocked the well-established
principles of recovery by saying that all we  are asking for is to sit around in groups and
sing “Kumbaya”. He says that he is rewriting international best practice on a day-by-day
basis, and that is actually what deeply dist urbs me. International best practice is based
on the evidence—the evidence that is gained from both successes and disasters. So
when there has been a failure of recovery, t hose lessons have been learnt and they are
available to us. This Government is placi ng a great risk on a Mi nister who wants to
rewrite history and rewrite our future.
When the Prime Minister spoke on 23 February, the day after our dreadful
earthquake, of which we acknowledge the anniversary next week, he said “On behalf of
the Government, let me be clear that no one will be left to walk this journey alone. New
Zealand will walk this journey with you. We  will be there every step of the way.
Christchurch; this is not your test, this is  New Zealand’s test. I promise we will meet
this test.” Today I am aski ng the Prime Minister and the Minister for Canterbury
Earthquake Recovery to meet the challenge that he quite rightly set the Government the
day after the disastrous earthqua ke. It is one week away from  that first anniversary, so I
know that I am going to be criticised for maki ng this statement, but I think it is really
important because there are people in Christ church who are extremely worried, not just
about the fact that this is the anniversary of the 22 February earthquake and they are still
out of their houses or face an uncertain future , but because it is nearly 18 months since
the first earthquake and some of them have  been out of their houses since the first
earthquake, and some of them still do not ha ve the basic services that we would expect
in a First World country. A number of them are facing the uncertainty of the land upon
which their houses are built, or facing an unpalatable choice between the Government’s
offer and the unknown. I want to talk about that, I want to talk about the red zone offer,
and I want to talk about the reality that people face about their land.
The first thing I want to mention, though, is how the Government has communicated
the land decisions, because I actually, persona lly, think there is nothing worse than the
15 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 425
way the Government has chosen to do it—by br iefing the media about the future of the
land, and not the people who are affected by the decisions. On 23 June 2011 the media
had already been briefed sufficiently to be  able to lead the front page of the  Press with
the decision that was going to be announced at lunchtime that day. As local MPs, we
were given a 15-minute heads-up of the deta il of the announcement. On 18 August the
Kaiapoi decisions were announced. Affected residents were denied admission to the
press conference where the future of their land was disclosed. On 19 August the details
of the red zone offer were launched immediately following the opening of the
Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority’s recovery assist ance centre. There were a
number of things about that announcement,  where the Government did not point out
that there was no right of appeal on the amount  of the offer—it did not mention that at
the press conference.
On 28 October most of the remaining orange  zones were turned green, but it did not
give any warning of these new foundation technical categories, 1, 2, and 3—1 being the
grey, 2 being the yellow, a nd 3 being the blue. Of cour se, that has caused major
concerns for a number of people who do not have the detail to go with that, requiring, as
it does, individual geotechnical site investig ations to determine foundation types. The
interesting thing about that announcement that day is that Brooklands residents who had
been on tenterhooks for months went online to  find out what was the story with their
community, and the system crashed. Guess what ? They had not change d colour at all,
and no one warned them that no decision ha d been made about Brooklands. This is
playing with people’s minds.
On 17 November a text message from the Mi nister’s office in the morning said there
would be announcements that afternoon. We we re briefed at 12 o’clock. At 2 o’clock
the people of Brooklands found out  that they were subject to  the red zone decision, but
they did not find out that that was going to happen until the press went out to ask them
for their response, how they felt about bei ng red-zoned. A lot of people in Brooklands
are very, very upset at that decision. Then  on February 10, again we had to contact the
Minister’s office to ask for details about the announcement. Again, Southshore was not
included, the white zones in my colleague’s electorate in Port Hills were not mentioned,
and, again, there was a great deal of uncertainty.
When I tell people this they are appalled at the insensitivity, and that is because, I
believe, the Government’s communication strategy is not focused on the affected
communities. It is political, and it is very inappropriate on every level. Because the
community does not understand the nature of  the decisions that are being made, they
therefore have no confidence in the quality of the decision making. When you have to
dig yourself out of silt on Christmas Eve,  Christmas Day, and Boxing Day, and you
have done it for the third time in a row, then you can understand why, in fact, there is no
confidence in the decision. This  is not just Parklands Ea st. All of the boundary areas
that we have been raising with the Government since July last year are all affected in the
same way and are asking for more details. Si gnificant numbers want to be red, but there
are also significant numbers in Brooklands that want to be green. And in Brooklands
they did not dig out tonnes of silt on 22 February, 13 June, or 23 December, because
their damage was done on 4 September.
If the Government had agreed to engage with them, as I have repeatedly asked month
after month after month, then people woul d understand what was happening. So many
people believe that the Cant erbury Earthquake Recovery Au thority makes the decision,
but it is not the authority; it  is the Government. It comes down to “What is the cost of
repair?”, and “How much are the sections wo rth?”. It is about m oney and it is about
insurance. The Government says the red zone offer has winners and losers. Well, it sure
does, and there are different shades of losers. I lose out  on what the Government has
426 Address in Reply 15 Feb 2012
described as an extremely fair deal, but I am not losing as much as many of the people I
am privileged to represent. I sat next to someone on the plane a while ago, and he asked
how my property was. I said I was in the re d zone, and he said: “O h, well, that’s lucky
for you.” I said: “Actually, I do not get enough out of the Government offer to buy what
I have got now”, and I also said that my in surance company had told me that it could
repair my house. But the point is, and the pers on sitting next to me said this: “But how
can they repair your house? You’re in the red zone.”
That is the problem. The Government has given in to the insurance industry and let it
off the hook for what we are entitled to. We signed up for replacement policies with our
insurers, and we expect the Government to stand by our si de, as the Prime Minister
promised us on 23 February, and enable us to move on with our lives—not to do any
better, we do not want to be winners; we ju st want to break even. That is not an
unreasonable thing for people to ask. That is what many people and the people of
Christchurch are asking the Government to unde rstand and to reflect on as we head into
this time. Maybe we could think about what the word “kumbaya” means. In the song it
says: “Someone’s crying Lord, kumbaya.” It means “come by here”, and maybe when
the Prime Minister is in Christchurch next week he would like to come by some of the
neighbourhoods and talk to them about the i ssues that are confr onting them and think
about whether the decision was the right one for Christchurch.

items.speaker: MOJO MATHERS
items.text: Tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou katoa. [In New
Zealand Sign Language]
Tōku awa, ko t ōku ora. T ōku awa, ko t ōku mana. Toku awa, ko t ōku kaha. T ōku
awa, ko tōku wairua.
[My river is my love, influence, strength, and spirituality.]
My river is my life.
It was the desire to save a very special rive r, the Waikirikiri, that led directly to my
involvement in politics. Twelve years ago I moved out of Chri stchurch to the village of
Coalgate in the foothills of  the Canterbury Plains with my former husband and three
small children. The location was ideal for us, close to a small country school, with the
peaceful Waikirikiri flowing past our door step, and amazing views of the mountains.
But shortly after moving there we found that  there were ambitious plans to build a
massive water storage dam for irrigation just upstream of us. If the dam went ahead the
beautiful Waikirikiri would become an ugly, fast-flowing canal, too dangerous for kids
to go swimming in. The dam would also de stroy private land protected by a Queen
Elizabeth the Second National Trust covenant , including two raised, spring-fed peat
bogs, which pollen analysis showed to be thous ands of years old. I recall standing with
my husband at the bottom of our property, looking upstream towards the Wairiri Valley,
wondering what we should do. Should we spend time and energy fighting the proposed
scheme or should we resign ourselves to it going ahead?
At that time we had a small business offering forestry management services, mainly
to farmers on the Canterbury Plains and foothills. We had witnessed firsthand the
devastating impact of prolonged drought. But we also knew that the scheme was not
about drought-proofing but about land intensification. It would allow ye t more farms to
convert to intensive dairying and dairy s upport—land uses dependent on high inputs of
energy, water, and fossil fuels. It was clear to us that our groundw ater and our rivers
were at risk. So we decided to try to stop the dam and hi ghlight to the wider public the
downside of intensive farming. As part of  this campaign we networked with other
committed people across Canterbury, all of us united by a desire to protect Canterbury’s
water. Some of this fight is covered in Sam Mahon’s book The Water Thieves.
It was during this time that I became dis illusioned with the po litics of both Labour
and National. It seemed to me that neither was willing or able to grasp the seriousness
15 Feb 2012 Address in Reply 427
of the threats facing our water. So, in part inspired by the late Rod Donald, who was my
neighbour prior to his election to Parliament , I joined the Green Party and stood as a
candidate for the first time in the 2005 general election.
When I first stood I had no concept of what  huge challenges lay ahead of me as a
deaf candidate and activist. I just wanted to speak out in defence of our water and our
environment and be heard. But I learnt the hard way that passion and knowledge were
not enough. I had to find different ways of doing politics, ways of getting around the
barriers posed by being deaf, ways that allowed me to participate and engage
effectively. I started learning New Zeala nd Sign Language and using sign language
interpreters when I s poke to submissions to the local city and re gional councils. I am
absolutely thrilled that there are New Zeal and Sign Language interpreters in the gallery
today, and I note that it is the first time in New Zealand that a maiden speech is being
covered this way. I hope that this will be th e start of greater recognition by Parliament
of the status of New Zealand Sign as our third official language.
I want to thank all those who campaigned to get New Zealand Sign Language Act
passed into law, and I acknowledge the role played by the former Minister for Disability
Issues the Hon Ruth Dyson in facilitating this process. The effects of this Act have been
positive for many, but there is still a long way to go before the Act is implemented as it
should be. For example, as a mother of th ree children I find it unacceptable that some
deaf parents are unable to at tend parent-teacher interviews to discuss their children’s
progress, as is their right, because th e school will not provide New Zealand Sign
Language interpreters.
I want to acknowledge the dedicated pe ople who campaigned for New Zealand to
sign and ratify the United Nations Conve ntion on the Rights of Persons with
Disabilities. New Zeala nd signed the convention on 30 March 2007 under a Labour
Government, and ratified it on 26 Sept ember 2008 under a National Government.
Article 29 of the convention guarantees the right of persons with  disabilities to
effectively and fully participate in politic al and public life, in cluding the right and
